title: No rare treat for a prince
literal_meaning: Is khaja an extraordinary treat for a king’s son?
explanation: Something impressive to one person may be ordinary to someone with easy access. The rhetorical question puts the proposed treat in perspective.
meaning_odia: ଜଣଙ୍କ ପାଇଁ ଖଜା ବହୁତ ଲୋଭନୀୟ ହୋଇପାରେ, ହେଲେ ସହଜରେ ତାହା ପାଉଥିବା ଜଣଙ୍କ ପାଇଁ ସେତେ ବିଶେଷ ନୁହେଁ। ସମାନ ଜିନିଷକୁ ନେଇ ଆଗ୍ରହ କାହିଁକି ଅଲଗା ହୁଏ, ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ସେହି ତଫାତକୁ ଧରେ। ନିଜକୁ ଯାହା ସାଧାରଣ ଲାଗେ, ଆଉ ଜଣଙ୍କ ପାଇଁ ତାହା ବଡ଼ ଆକର୍ଷଣ ହୋଇପାରେ।
usage_example: An experienced photographer is unlikely to be dazzled simply by being shown a camera. (New editorial example, not a collected quotation.)
cultural_context: Khaja remains the named sweet. The source gloss explains ready access; no particular prince or court incident is identified.

odia: ଲୁଣ ଖାଇବା ଯାହାର, ଗୁଣ ଗାଇ ତାହାର
title: Whose salt, whose praise?
literal_meaning: Eat someone’s salt; sing that person’s merits.
explanation: Salt stands for livelihood received through service in the dictionary definition. The line links material dependence with praise of the provider. It may express loyalty, or make a sharp comment about praise shaped by dependence; the occasion decides the force. It does not establish that every employee’s praise is dishonest or that support requires silence.
meaning_odia: ଏଠି ଲୁଣ ଖାଇବା କେବଳ ଖାଦ୍ୟର କଥା ନୁହେଁ; ଅଭିଧାନରେ ଏହା କାହା ଅଧୀନରେ ଚାକିରି କରି ଜୀବିକା ଚଳାଇବା। ଯାହାଠାରୁ ଜୀବିକା ମିଳେ ତାହାର ପ୍ରଶଂସା କରିବା ସହ କଥାଟି ଯୋଡ଼େ। କେବେ ଏହା ଆନୁଗତ୍ୟର କଥା, କେବେ ନିର୍ଭରତା ପାଇଁ ହେଉଥିବା ପ୍ରଶଂସାକୁ ଟାହି। ସବୁ କର୍ମଚାରୀଙ୍କ ପ୍ରଶଂସା ମିଛ କିମ୍ବା ସାହାଯ୍ୟ ନେଲେ ଚୁପ୍ ରହିବାକୁ ହେବ ବୋଲି ଅର୍ଥ ନୁହେଁ।
english_summary: The salt image connects livelihood with loyalty—or praise shaped by dependence.
odia_summary: ଜୀବିକା ଓ ପ୍ରଶଂସାର ସମ୍ପର୍କକୁ ଲୁଣର ଛବି ଧରେ।
usage_example: After hearing an adviser praise every decision of the person who pays them, a listener quietly repeats the line. (Original imagined example, not collected testimony.)
cultural_context: Service meaning is sourced; two possible conversational tones are editorial. Companion refusal wording is recorded separately, not counted as another saying.

odia: କେତେ ଅନଉଛୁ ମତେ, ତୋଠଉଁ ସୁନ୍ଦର ମୋର ବିନୋଦିଆ, ଚାକର ରଖିବ ତତେ
title: A boast that puts the onlooker in place
literal_meaning: Why keep looking at me? My charming one is more beautiful than you and could keep you as a servant.
explanation: The line answers someone who keeps looking at the speaker by praising another person as more beautiful. The dictionary explains “keep as a servant” here as figurative superiority in wealth or qualities, so the comparison is not a report of employment. One possible performance is a proud rebuff to an admirer: the speaker boasts that a favoured person would far outshine this supposed rival. Neither admiration nor a romantic relationship is fixed by the source gloss, however. The repeated address gives the comparison a personal, theatrical edge. Its status hierarchy is part of the rhetoric, not a measure of anyone’s human worth.
meaning_odia: କେହି ଚାହିଁରହିଥିବା ବେଳେ ଏହି କଥାର ବକ୍ତା ନିଜ ପ୍ରିୟଜଣଙ୍କ ସୁନ୍ଦରତାକୁ ବଢ଼ାଇ କହି ସେହି ଚାହାଣିର ଜବାବ ଦିଅନ୍ତି। ଚାକର ରଖିବାକୁ ଅଭିଧାନ ଏଠାରେ ଧନ ବା ଗୁଣରେ ଉତ୍କୃଷ୍ଟ ହେବାର ଲକ୍ଷଣାର୍ଥ ଦେଇଛି। ଯିଏ ନିଜକୁ ପ୍ରତିଦ୍ୱନ୍ଦ୍ୱୀ ଭାବୁଥାଇପାରେ, ତାକୁ ପ୍ରିୟଜଣଙ୍କଠାରୁ ବହୁତ ତଳେ ରଖିଦେବାରେ ଏହି ଉତ୍ତରର ଖୋଚା। ଏହା ନିଜ ପ୍ରିୟଜଣଙ୍କୁ ନେଇ ଗର୍ବ ସାଙ୍ଗରେ ମିଶିଥିବା ଏକ ନାଟକୀୟ ଜବାବ ଭଳି ଶୁଣାଯାଏ; ପ୍ରେମର ପରିସ୍ଥିତି ଏହାର ଗୋଟିଏ ସମ୍ଭାବ୍ୟ ପାଠ। କାମ ବା ସାମାଜିକ ସ୍ଥିତି ଦେଇ ମଣିଷର ମୂଲ୍ୟ ମାପିବାକୁ ଏହି ପାଠ ସମର୍ଥନ କରେନାହିଁ।
english_summary: A pointed comparison answers an onlooker with a boast about someone else’s beauty.
odia_summary: ନିଜ ପ୍ରିୟଜଣଙ୍କ ଗର୍ବ କରି ଚାହିଁରହିଥିବା ଜଣକୁ ଖୋଚା ଦେଉଥିବା ଉତ୍ତର।
usage_example: Original imagined example: During a light-hearted drama rehearsal, one character keeps posing to catch another character’s eye. The other quotes this line, praising someone supposedly more beautiful. The performers choose to play it as a proud rebuff to an admirer; that relationship is invented for this scene, not established by the dictionary. They treat the employment comparison as exaggeration rather than a reason to mock an occupation.
cultural_context: The source supplies a figurative status comparison, not a named romance or biographical episode. Charming one renders ବିନୋଦିଆ without fixing a romantic relationship; the speaker’s gender and any historical characters are not established. The employment hierarchy should remain visible as rhetoric without being endorsed.

odia: ଢିଙ୍କି ପଡ଼େ ଧମଧମ, ସାହାବ ଚାକିରି ଭାରି କଠିଣ; ଝାଳ ବୁହେ ଗମଗମ
title: The sound and sweat of work
literal_meaning: The dheṅki falls thump-thump; service to the sahib is very hard; sweat streams.
explanation: The heavy beat of the pounding implement is answered by the sound of streaming sweat. Between them comes the complaint that service to the sahib is hard. Sound makes the labour felt before any abstract judgment is offered. The line can be read as a rhythmic complaint about demanding work, but the quotation does not identify an employer, worker or event. A present-day speaker may borrow its exaggerated beat to describe a tiring task; that is a new use, not evidence of a particular historical labour arrangement.
meaning_odia: ଢିଙ୍କିର “ଧମଧମ” ଶବ୍ଦ ପରେ ଝାଳର “ଗମଗମ” ଆସୁଛି। ମଝିରେ ସାହାବଙ୍କ ଚାକିରି କେତେ କଠିନ, ସେ ଅଭିଯୋଗ ରହିଛି। ଶବ୍ଦର ତାଳରେ କାମର ଭାର ଓ ଶରୀରର କ୍ଳାନ୍ତି ଏକାଠି ଶୁଣାଯାଏ। ଆଜି କେହି ନିଜର କଠିନ କାମକୁ ନେଇ ଏହା କହିଲେ ପୁରୁଣା ଚିତ୍ରଟି ନୂଆ ପ୍ରସଙ୍ଗକୁ ଆସେ; କିନ୍ତୁ ମୂଳ ପଦର କର୍ମୀ ବା ସାହାବଙ୍କ ପରିଚୟ ଆମ ପାଖରେ ନାହିଁ।
english_summary: Thumping sound and streaming sweat turn a complaint about hard service into a rhythmic line.
odia_summary: ଢିଙ୍କିର ଶବ୍ଦ ଓ ଝାଳର ଚିତ୍ରରେ କଠିନ ଚାକିରିର ଅଭିଯୋଗ ତାଳ ପାଏ।
usage_example: Original imagined example: After repeatedly moving heavy boxes for a demanding organiser, a volunteer recites the line to a friend, tapping out “ଧମଧମ.” The friend hears both the joke and the complaint about the workload.
cultural_context: Source label is Dhaga under an onomatopoeic word. The term sahib is retained as an unspecified form of address/status in the quotation; no colonial employer, date, caste or documented work scene is inferred. Not identical to048 compulsory work wherever one goes.

title: A face praised, a body judged
literal_meaning: The face is beautiful; the body is ugly.
explanation: The parallel halves divide one person into a praised face and a disparaged body. The dictionary places the last word under “ugly,” not its other senses of a lump or something flat. Our critical reading asks what this splitting does to the person being described. The source supplies the appearance judgment; our objection to reducing someone to it is editorial.
meaning_odia: ସମାନ ଢାଞ୍ଚାର ଦୁଇ ଖଣ୍ଡ ଜଣେ ମଣିଷକୁ ପ୍ରଶଂସିତ ମୁହଁ ଓ ନିନ୍ଦିତ ଦେହରେ ବାଣ୍ଟେ। ଅଭିଧାନ ଶେଷ ଶବ୍ଦକୁ ଅସୁନ୍ଦର ଅର୍ଥରେ ରଖିଛି, ମେଞ୍ଚା ବା ଚେପ୍ଟା ଅର୍ଥରେ ନୁହେଁ। ଆମ ସମାଲୋଚନାତ୍ମକ ପଢ଼ା ପଚାରେ—ଏହି ବାଣ୍ଟିବା ବର୍ଣ୍ଣିତ ଲୋକଟିକୁ କେଉଁଠି ରଖେ? ରୂପର ରାୟ ଉତ୍ସରେ ଅଛି; ମଣିଷକୁ ସେତିକିରେ ସୀମିତ କରିବା ପ୍ରତି ଆପତ୍ତି ଆମର।
english_summary: Our critical reading questions dividing a person into praised and disparaged features.
odia_summary: ପ୍ରଶଂସା ଓ ନିନ୍ଦାର ଅଙ୍ଗରେ ମଣିଷକୁ ବାଣ୍ଟିବା ପ୍ରତି ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ।
usage_example: Original imagined example: A reading group discusses appearance-based remarks. One participant quotes the line; another asks how the person described might feel hearing praise immediately turned into an insult. This imagined discussion questions the judgment rather than describing an actual person.
cultural_context: A short dictionary-labelled expression, not a diagnosis or objective measure of beauty. No gender, body type or community is assigned beyond what the wording establishes.
